LaRue County sits in central Kentucky, with Hodgenville as the county seat. It is best known as the birthplace of Abraham Lincoln. For investors, the county matters because Kentucky sells delinquent real property taxes as tax lien certificates, called certificates of delinquency, through the county clerk. This guide explains how LaRue County tax sales work, what the recent notice showed, how registration and bidding work, and what steps investors should take before buying.

What is LaRue County’s tax lien investing system?

LaRue County follows Kentucky’s certificate of delinquency system. That means the county clerk sells delinquent real property tax bills to approved buyers instead of selling the real estate itself at this stage. The buyer gets a lien position tied to the unpaid taxes, not immediate ownership of the property. In LaRue County, the official clerk page lists delinquent taxes and posts the annual in person sale notice.

Important Details

Key Takeaways

  • LaRue County, Kentucky, utilizes a tax lien investing system where tax delinquency certificates are sold instead of properties.
  • Investors must register for the auction at least 30 days in advance and pay a fee to participate in the tax lien sales.
  • The auction process involves a random draw and allows priority claim holders to select liens first, ensuring a structured selection.
  • Due diligence is critical for investors to avoid risks like investing in low-value parcels or misunderstanding ownership rights.
  • Kentucky offers opportunities for both local and foreign investors to buy liens, including over-the-counter purchases after the auction.

Fun Facts About the County

  • LaRue County was created in 1843 and Hodgenville is the county seat.
  • Abraham Lincoln was born in what is now LaRue County.
  • The county’s population was estimated at about 15,184 in 2025.
  • Agriculture remains a big part of the local economy. Recent county agriculture materials reported more than $60 million in production.

Attractions & Economic Highlights

  • Abraham Lincoln Birthplace National Historical Park is the county’s best known historic site.
  • Main travel access includes Lincoln Parkway, US 31E, US 31W, and nearby I 65 connections.
  • Agriculture is a leading local industry, with schools and regional commuting also shaping the economy.
  • Outdoor time, local festivals, and Lincoln themed tourism add to the county’s appeal.

Why This County is Ideal for Tax Lien Investors

  • Kentucky tax lien certificates can produce high returns because the lien accrues 1% per month after purchase.
  • LaRue County posts its sale through the county clerk, which gives investors a clear county level source to monitor.
  • The county is small enough to research by hand, which can help reduce mistakes. This is a low risk investment only when due diligence is strong. That part is the real edge.
  • Kentucky also allows unsold certificates to be bought after the sale, which can help investors who miss auction day.

Auction Process for Tax Lien Sales

LaRue County runs an in person county clerk sale for certificates of delinquency. The recent county notice set the sale at the courthouse at 9:00 AM Eastern. Registration is not optional. Buyers must submit the county form, the required lists, fees, and deposits by the posted deadline. State rules say the clerk posts the sale details and tax list at least 30 days before the sale.

Kentucky does not use an interest bid down format for these county clerk sales. The interest on the certificate is set by law after purchase. The sale works more like a selection process among registered buyers. Priority claims are handled first. Then the rest of the certificates are chosen through rounds after a random drawing decides order.

How the Auction Works

  1. Register before the deadline

    Submit Form 62A374, your certificate list, registration fee, and deposits by the county’s cutoff. Recent LaRue notice required all items by August 8 for an August 19 sale.

  2. Report to the clerk on sale day

    Registered buyers report to the county clerk for instructions on where the sale is held. The available list may change right up to sale time if owners pay.

  3. Priority liens go first

    If you already hold a prior year certificate on the same property, Kentucky gives you first priority on the current year certificate if you filed it correctly.

  4. Random order controls selection

    The clerk uses a random drawing to set buyer order. That order carries through each round.

  5. Buyers choose from pre filed lists

    You may select only certificates that were on your submitted list. Counties can sell in small lots, and many clerks start one certificate at a time for the early rounds.

  6. Pay the balance after the sale

    Your deposit is applied to the total due. Any extra deposit left after the sale is refunded within 10 business days.

Maximum Potential Returns and Expected Returns on LaRue County Tax Lien Certificates

For LaRue County tax lien certificates, the stated return is tied to Kentucky law, not bidding pressure. After purchase, the certificate accrues simple interest at 1% per month, or 12% per year, and certain added fees may also be recoverable under state rules.

Expected returns depend on how fast the owner redeems, whether notices are handled correctly, and whether the certificate ever moves into foreclosure. The highest real world outcomes usually come when a lien redeems with interest and allowed costs, or when enforcement is done correctly after the waiting period. The main limit is time, paperwork, and property quality.

Open to All Investors and Foreign Investor Participation

Kentucky’s rules focus on registration, deadlines, and payment requirements. The rules do not say that only local LaRue County residents may buy. In practice, that means out of county and out of state investors can join if they meet the state and county registration rules.

The same reading suggests foreign investors may also participate, because the system is based on purchaser registration rather than local residency. That said, foreign buyers should confirm entity structure, tax reporting, payment method, and legal service needs before bidding. That is an inference from the registration framework, not a separate county rule posted by LaRue County.

Importance of Due Diligence in LaRue County Tax Lien Investing

What Due Diligence Entails

  • Check the parcel, owner name, and tax amount on the county list.
  • Review PVA and map data before you register your target certificates.
  • Drive by the property or get fresh photos. Rural parcels can fool online buyers.
  • Check access, flood issues, use limits, and occupancy risk.
  • Know that you are buying a lien, not the house itself.

Risks of Skipping Due Diligence

  • You may tie up money in weak parcels with little resale value.
  • You may miss notice steps that affect fees or enforcement rights.
  • You may assume you can take possession right away, which is wrong in a lien state.
  • You may spend legal fees on a certificate that never fits your exit plan.

Buying Over the Counter Liens in LaRue County

How to Purchase OTC Liens

Kentucky allows any remaining certificates of delinquency to be bought after the tax sale. State guidance says that once the county sale is complete, unsold certificates may be purchased at any time by any qualified third party purchaser, subject to continuing registration rules and county fees. In plain terms, if LaRue County has leftovers after sale day, those can work like over the counter liens.

Benefits of OTC Purchases

OTC style purchases remove the pressure of sale day. You can review the list more calmly and avoid fighting for the same small group of certificates. The tradeoff is simple. The best liens may already be gone.

Why LaRue County is a Top Choice for Tax Lien Investors

Economic and Tax Advantages

  • Central Kentucky location gives easy road access to research trips.
  • Agriculture and regional commuting support the local economy.
  • Kentucky’s tax lien system gives a known statutory return instead of a bid down yield.

Real Estate Market Overview

LaRue County is a smaller rural market. That can help investors who prefer a manageable list over a huge metro auction. It also means property level research matters more. A good lien on a useful parcel can be solid. A bad lien on a weak parcel can sit for a long time. In counties like LaRue, the buyer who researches better often does better.

Conclusion

LaRue County, Kentucky is a county clerk tax lien market, not a county tax deed market. The sale is usually held in the late summer window used across Kentucky, and recent official dates for LaRue fell in mid August. The recent county notice also showed an in person courthouse sale at 9:00 AM Eastern with advance registration, fees, and deposits required.

The real appeal is the structure. Buyers get a certificate of delinquency with 1% monthly simple interest after purchase, plus a path to collection or foreclosure if the lien is not paid and the legal waiting period has passed. Still, smart investing here means doing full research before you register targets. Good paperwork and good property review matter just as much as the return.

Pro Tips

  • Focus first on parcels you can inspect fast from Hodgenville and the main road corridors. It saves time on rural research trips.
  • Build your certificate list early. LaRue uses pre submitted lists, so last minute ideas do not help much.
  • Watch the clerk page close to sale day. Owners can still pay before the auction starts.
  • Treat small county liens like a paperwork game. Clean notice work protects interest and fee rights.
  • Check whether leftovers remain after the sale. In Kentucky, unsold certificates can still be bought later.

FAQs for LaRue County Tax Liens

Do I get the property right after the sale?

No. You buy a tax lien certificate, not the deed.

When can foreclosure start?

State guidance says no enforcement action until at least one year after delinquency.

Can I enter or renovate the property?

No. Not unless you later gain ownership through the legal process.

What happens if the owner pays?

You receive payoff under Kentucky’s lien rules, including statutory interest and allowed charges.

Can I sell or assign the certificate later?

Kentucky allows assignment of certificates between qualified parties
